For an oriented surface $S$, the transported power is defined by

$$
P_S = \int_S \mathbf{q} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\,dA
$$

where $\mathbf{q}$ is the heat-flux vector, $P_S$ is the crossing power in
W, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the chosen unit normal, and $dA$ is a surface
element in m$^2$. The [parallel heat flux](name:parallel_heat_flux) is its
projection along the local magnetic-field direction. Convective transport
may be parameterized by the ratio of heat flux to product of particle flux
and particle temperature due to convection.

Sign convention: Positive when the local component of $\mathbf{q}$ points
along the chosen oriented surface normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$.

items.name: outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment
items.description:
Radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative geometry radius used to
define its outer boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed
cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame about the toroidal symmetry axis.
items.documentation:
Radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative geometry radius that
defines the outer boundary of an annular iron-core region. This member
specializes radius of an iron-core segment to the outermost boundary
measured from the toroidal symmetry axis. The relevant cross-section is the
plane spanned by $R$ and $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$
frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis
and $Z$ is vertical height.

The outer radius is the maximum major-radius coordinate on the
cross-sectional boundary:

$$
r_{\rm out} = \max_{(R,Z)\in\partial A} R
$$

where $r_{\rm out}$ is the outer radius, $A$ is the iron-core
cross-sectional region, and $\partial A$ is its boundary; $R$, $Z$, and
$r_{\rm out}$ are expressed in meters.

For annular geometry, the outer radius together with the [inner radius of an
iron-core segment](name:inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment) determines the
radial thickness through $r_{\rm out}-r_{\rm in}$. It is an axis-referenced
outer extent, not the radius of a local circular arc about an explicit
off-axis center or the full rectangular extent described by the [width of an
iron-core segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment).

items.name: hydrogen_density_at_divertor_target
items.description:
Number density of the hydrogen species at the divertor target is the local
particle count per volume for hydrogen ions at the sheath entrance, summed
over positive charge states and excluding neutral hydrogen atoms and
molecules.
items.documentation:
Number density of the hydrogen species at the divertor target is the local
particle count per volume at the sheath entrance immediately upstream of the
target-facing plasma boundary. It is the hydrogen-specific member of
[density_at_divertor_target](name:density_at_divertor_target).

The local hydrogen-ion number density is defined by the differential
particle count:

$$
n_{\mathrm{H}} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{H}}}{dV}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the number of free hydrogen ions in a small plasma
volume $V$ whose center approaches the sheath entrance from the plasma side
at the divertor target, and $n_{\mathrm{H}}$ is the corresponding local
hydrogen-ion number density.

This quantity applies to the free hydrogen-ion population immediately
adjacent to the divertor target. It is summed over all positive hydrogen
ionization charge states, counting each ion once without charge weighting;
neutral hydrogen atoms and molecules, electrons, and other ion species are
excluded.

As a species-specific local component, it uses the same sheath-entrance
locus and charge-state-summed convention as [deuterium density at the
divertor target](name:deuterium_density_at_divertor_target), but represents
hydrogen ions rather than deuterium ions. Unlike the flux-surface-averaged
hydrogen density at the plasma boundary, it is evaluated locally at the
divertor target rather than averaged over a flux surface.

items.name: helium_4_density
items.description:
Local number density of helium-4 ions per unit plasma volume, the principal
measure of fusion ash concentration in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas.
items.documentation:
The helium-4 ion number density $n_{{}^4\text{He}}$ quantifies the local
concentration of ${}^4\text{He}$ nuclei at a given point in the plasma. At
fusion-relevant temperatures (several keV), helium-4 is fully stripped to
He$^{2+}$, and in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas it accumulates as the
primary fusion ash product of the reaction ${}^2\text{H} + {}^3\text{H}
\rightarrow {}^4\text{He} + n$; its buildup dilutes the fuel and reduces the
fusion reaction rate if not exhausted by the divertor system.

The time evolution of $n_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is governed by the particle
continuity equation

$$
\frac{\partial n_{{}^4\text{He}}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{{}^4\text{He}} = S_{{}^4\text{He}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is the helium-4 particle flux
and $S_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is the volumetric source rate from fusion reactions
and ionization of recycled helium neutrals at the plasma edge.

The helium-4 density is measured primarily via charge exchange recombination
spectroscopy, where injected neutral beam atoms undergo charge exchange with
He$^{2+}$ ions to produce line emission from excited helium atoms; passive
spectroscopy of edge recycling emission provides a complementary approach.
Chord-averaged and volume-averaged forms are provided by
[line_averaged_helium_4_density](name:line_averaged_helium_4_density) and
[volume_averaged_helium_4_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_4_density)
respectively, while
[helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary)
gives the boundary value.

In D-T burning plasmas, central He-4 densities are in the range
$10^{18}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, with the helium-to-electron density ratio —
captured by
[fraction](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_helium_4_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density)
— kept below approximately 5-10% in steady state to avoid excessive fuel
dilution.

items.name: spectral_signal_to_noise_ratio_of_spectrometer_channel
items.description:
Spectrometer-channel spectral signal-to-noise ratio is the scalar comparison
of spectral power integrated over a selected signal wavelength interval with
spectral power integrated over a line-free reference interval for the same
channel. It names the shared signal/reference comparison; scale-specific
child names define the numerical mapping.
items.documentation:
Spectrometer-channel spectral signal-to-noise ratio is the scalar comparison
between selected spectral signal content and a line-free spectral reference
for one spectrometer channel. Its physical content is the comparison of
spectral power integrated over a selected signal wavelength interval with
spectral power integrated over a selected line-free reference wavelength
interval for the same channel.

The scale-specific value is determined from the integrated spectral-power
ratio:

$$
q = F\!\left(\frac{P_{\mathrm{sig}}}{P_{\mathrm{ref}}}\right)
$$

where $q$ is the spectrometer-channel spectral signal-to-noise ratio value,
$F$ is the numerical scale mapping specified by the scale-specific member,
$P_{\mathrm{sig}}$ is the spectral power integrated over the selected signal
wavelength interval, and $P_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the spectral power integrated
over the selected line-free reference wavelength interval for the same
spectrometer channel.

The scope is one spectrometer channel and one selected pair of wavelength
intervals. The aggregation convention is to integrate spectral power over
each interval before applying $F$; the numerator is the signal interval and
the denominator is the line-free reference interval. The reference interval
supplies the noise/reference comparison and is not a second signal interval.

This quantity is not an absolute spectral power, a pointwise spectral power
density, a raw detector response, or a comparison between different
spectrometer channels. As a parent quantity, it denotes the common
signal/reference spectral-power comparison shared by scale-specific
children; the [logarithmic spectral signal-to-noise ratio of a spectrometer
channel](name:spectral_signal_to_noise_ratio_logarithm_of_spectrometer_channel)
is the member that fixes $F$ to base-ten logarithmic scaling of the same
integrated-power ratio.
